title: Perfective and imperfective
goal: Face the one part of Slovak with no real equivalent in English: every action has two verbs, and choosing the wrong one changes the meaning of your sentence.
bekal: understand what the perfective/imperfective pair really distinguishes — and that it isn't time
recognize pairs from their shape: a prefix, a change in the middle, or a completely different word
choose the right form in past and future sentences

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Prečo si to nedočítal?
dialogs.intro: Eva lent Budi a book last week. Now she wants it back.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Čítal si tú knihu, čo som ti dala?
lines.id: Have you read the book I gave you?
lines.literal: read-m you-are that book, which I-am to-you given-f?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I've been reading it, but I haven't finished.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nie je! Každý večer som čítal desať strán.
lines.id: It's not! I read ten pages every evening.
lines.literal: not is! every evening I-am read-m ten pages-gen.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.id: And will you finish it today?

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Dobre. A čo si varil včera?
lines.id: OK. And what did you cook yesterday?
lines.literal: good. and what you-are cooked-m yesterday?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Varil som dve hodiny a nič som neuvaril.
lines.id: I cooked for two hours and nothing turned out.
lines.literal: cooked-m I-am two hours-pl and nothing I-am not-cooked-done-m.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Zabudol som kúpiť ryžu. Kupoval som všetko ostatné.
lines.id: I forgot to buy rice. I bought everything else.
lines.literal: forgotten-m I-am buy rice-acc. bought-m I-am all rest.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nakoniec som zjedol dve porcie v jedálni.
lines.id: In the end I ate two portions at the canteen.
lines.literal: finally I-am eaten-up-m two portions in canteen-loc.

notes: **Čítal som ju, ale neprečítal.** One sentence that holds this whole unit. *Čítal* = I spent time reading it (the activity really happened). *Neprečítal* = I didn't get to the last page (the result wasn't reached). Both are about the past, and both are true in the same sentence.

**Varil som dve hodiny a nič som neuvaril.** Same pattern, and this time it's even funny. The cooking went on for two full hours — that's *varil*. But no dish came out of it — that's *neuvaril*. In English you need extra words to separate the two; Slovak does it with one prefix.

**Kupoval som všetko ostatné, ale zabudol som kúpiť ryžu.** *Kupoval* = the activity of shopping (walking around, filling the basket). *Kúpiť* = getting one particular item. Because the rice never made it into the basket, the perfective is used — and it's negated.

**Zjedol som dve porcie** uses the perfective because the portions were really finished. Compare *Jedol som* = "I was eating / I ate (for a while)". The prefix *z-* here means "all the way, until it's gone".

**The perfective can't be paired with a length of time.** *Varil som dve hodiny* is right; *Uvaril som dve hodiny* means nothing. If your sentence says how long, the verb must be imperfective. A quick check that saves a lot of sentences.

grammars.title: What is really being distinguished
body: Not time. Not politeness. Not quantity. What's distinguished is whether you see the action as **an ongoing activity** or as **a completed event**.
after: **The third row is the key to the whole system.** The perfective **has no present**, because "being in the middle of finishing" isn't a possible state. Since the form still exists grammatically but has no job in the present, it's used for the future. That's the full explanation for what you saw in unit 14.

**English expresses something similar, but with extra words**: "read" and "read to the end", "cook" and "get it cooked", "study" and "master". Slovak builds the difference into the verb itself, and makes you choose every time.

**At A1, one practical rule covers most sentences:** if there's a word like *často, každý deň, väčšinou, dve hodiny, celý deň* — use the imperfective. If there's *raz, konečne, už, hneď* — use the perfective. The time word in the sentence almost always gives you the answer.

grammars.title: Three ways pairs are formed
body: You can recognize perfective/imperfective pairs by their shape. There are three patterns, and the first covers the most words.
after: **The first pattern is the most common, and the prefixes aren't decoration.** *U-, na-, pre-, z-, vy-, za-* each have their own meaning — *pre-* means "all the way through", *vy-* means "out / until it's gone", *z-* means "into being / away". But when they form a perfective pair, the extra meaning fades until you can barely feel it.

**The third pattern explains pairs that look like they make no sense.** *Hľadať* (look for) and *nájsť* (find) are two completely different words in English, but in Slovak they're the imperfective–perfective pair of the same action: looking is the process, finding is the result. Once you see it that way, the pair feels natural.

**Write pairs down together from now on.** If you learn *robiť* on its own, you can say "I'm working on it" but not "I'll get it done". The glossary at the back of this book lists them in pairs, and that's no accident.

sections.title: Choosing correctly — six pairs of sentences

blocks.text: The fastest way to understand this system isn't through rules but through pairs of sentences that differ by just one prefix. Read both out loud and feel the difference.

head: Imperfective
Perfective
The difference
rows: was writing / the letter is done
was drinking / the coffee is gone
was studying / now I know it
worked on it a long time / it's done

blocks.text: **Look at the fourth row.** *Učil som sa* means you sat and studied; *naučil som sa* means you can now do it. That's why *Učím sa po slovensky* (I'm learning Slovak) is right, but *Naučím sa po slovensky* means "I will master Slovak" — a much bigger promise.

blocks.title: Three places that are always imperfective
items: **After *začať* (start), *prestať* (stop), *pokračovať* (continue)**: *Začal som čítať*, not *začal som prečítať*. You can't "start finishing".
**When there's a length of time**: *dve hodiny, celý deň, celý týždeň*. The perfective has no duration.
**When there's a frequency**: *často, každý deň, väčšinou, niekedy, vždy*. A repeated action is, by definition, never completed.

blocks.title: Two places that are almost always perfective
items: **When there's *už* (already) or *konečne* (finally)**: *Už som to urobil*, *Konečne som ju prečítal*.
**When the action happens once and the result matters**: *Kúpil som lístok*, *Zaplatil som*, *Prišiel som*. Almost every everyday sentence about something getting done belongs here.

blocks.text: Learn them in pairs, not one by one. The third column is the *ja* form of the perfective — the form that means the future.

If you only have time to learn half, learn **the second and third columns**. The perfective is what you'll need most in everyday conversation, because most of what you talk about is something that's already done or will get done.
